title: How Zippers Work: The Tiny Y That Locks Every Tooth

chapters.CH1: TWO ROWS, HALF A TOOTH APART

lines.say: A zipper has no lock, no hook, and no glue.
And yet it holds.
The secret is hidden inside this tiny slider.
In four minutes: two rows of teeth that never line up...
...and one tiny Y that makes them lock.
Let's start with the teeth.
Open a zipper: two tapes, each edged with a row of teeth.
Look closely. <break time="0.4s"/> The two rows don't match: one is shifted by half a tooth.
So every tooth on one side faces a gap on the other.
If the teeth lined up, they would hit head-on. <break time="0.4s"/> Shifted, each one slips in between two.
Closed, a common chain is only about five millimetres wide.
Every tooth sits between two neighbours. But that alone holds nothing.
So what does one tooth actually look like?
On top, a small bump. <break time="0.4s"/> Underneath, a hollow.
The bump of one tooth drops into the hollow of the next, like nested spoons.
And the head of each tooth is wider than the gap it sits in. <break time="0.4s"/> Pull the tapes sideways, and nothing slides out.
But that same shape causes a problem. Push two rows straight together...
...and they jam. The wide heads can't get past each other.
So how does a slider do what your fingers can't?
Let's look inside one.
Make the slider transparent, and you find a channel shaped like a Y.
Two arms in at the top, one way out at the bottom, and a divider in between.
Each row of teeth runs down one arm.
As the arms close in, the channel bends the chain very slightly, and the teeth tilt.
That tilt is the whole trick. <break time="0.4s"/> A tilted tooth clears the head of the one ahead of it...
...then it straightens, and its bump drops into the hollow. <break time="0.4s"/> Click.
Then the next one. And the next. Again and again, all the way up.
The walls of the Y do the pushing, at the same angle, every time.
Your fingers can't do that. The slider does it for you.
So what happens when you pull it down?
That divider in the middle is a wedge. <break time="0.4s"/> It pushes between the teeth and pries them apart.
And because the wedge has to stay between the last two teeth, no zipper is ever completely closed.
Stops at both ends keep the slider from running off the chain.
And the pull tab is more than a handle. <break time="0.4s"/> On many sliders, when it lies flat, a small pin drops between the teeth and holds the slider.
Up, the Y locks the teeth. <break time="0.4s"/> Down, the wedge opens them.
Not every zipper has separate teeth, though.
Coil zippers, the most common kind, use a plastic thread wound into a spiral, one on each tape.
Molded zippers have plastic teeth formed right onto the edge of the tape.
And metal teeth are cut from wire, stamped with their bump and hollow, and clamped on, one by one.
Three ways to make teeth. One slider.
In eighteen ninety-three, a Chicago inventor patented a shoe fastener made of hooks.
Twenty years later, an engineer swapped the hooks for teeth that nest into each other. The patent came in nineteen seventeen.
The name came in nineteen twenty-three, from rubber boots <break time="0.4s"/> and the sound they made. Zip.
So why do zippers fail?
Lose a single tooth...
...and its neighbours have nothing left to hold. The chain opens, tooth after tooth.
More often, it's the slider. With wear, its mouth spreads a little, and the rows slip apart behind it.
The fix: squeeze the slider very gently with pliers, until the teeth lock again.
Stuck instead? Rub a pencil on the teeth. Graphite is a dry lubricant.
Two rows, half a tooth apart.
One tiny Y. And it holds.
